analysis.one_liner: Caps monthly natural gas price increases to end users at 15 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee, dying without a markup, floor vote, or hearing before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Natural Gas Act so that any sale of natural gas in interstate commerce where the price charged to an end user rises more than 15 percent in a single month is automatically deemed "not just and unreasonable" under federal law [S2][S3]. That gives federal regulators a legal hook to reject or roll back price spikes hitting households and businesses that buy gas directly. It was introduced in May 2001 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2003 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas and face sharp monthly price increases. The bill would make any end-user price increase above 15 percent in one month legally challengeable as unjust and unreasonable, giving regulators a tool against sudden spikes [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and businesses facing gas price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Declares that any end-user natural gas rate increase exceeding 15 percent per month is deemed not just and unreasonable under the Natural Gas Act [S2][S3].
Applies to sales in interstate commerce of natural gas to end users, adding a new consumer-protection standard to Section 4(a) of the Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas sellers and utilities serving end users, who would lose the ability to raise prices freely during tight markets and could have excessive charges struck down by regulators [S3].

drawbacks.text: A fixed 15 percent monthly threshold is blunt: it treats a modest compounding run-up the same as a genuine emergency, and in long-running tight markets it could block price increases that reflect real supply costs [S3].

Capping price increases below what markets would bear can discourage investment in new supply at exactly the moment shortages hit, potentially making gas harder to find and rationing the effect instead of the price [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real but narrow and bluntly designed. It only triggers on monthly increases above 15 percent, so it does not cap prices overall — it only targets the steepest spikes. The honest objection is the classic one against price ceilings: in a genuine shortage, holding prices down may leave suppliers with less incentive to bring gas to market. But a rule that keeps charges from doubling in a single month is a limited safeguard, not a full price control, and the cost to suppliers would fall only during extreme run-ups. The design is workable if imperfect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bennie Thompson introduced the bill on May 15, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
A week later, on May 22, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas sellers and utilities, which keep the freedom to raise end-user prices without a monthly limit; households facing spikes got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas sellers, untouched by any cap

for.name: 4 of 208 House Democrats and 1 of 1 House Independents

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the subcommittee on May 22, 2001, and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no House Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Natural gas sellers and utilities serving end users
industries.note: A monthly 15 percent cap on end-user price increases would limit their ability to charge whatever tight markets allow, exposing extreme charges to being struck down as unjust and unreasonable. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against consumers facing spikes.
